template_name: Multi-Sensory Spatial Coherence in Architectural Environments
scope_correction: Per PRE_PANEL_REVIEW_CLEARANCE_MULTI_I.md: this template concerns multi-sensory spatial coherence, NOT social cognition. The Sprint Task Brief description was erroneous.

mechanism_chain.process: Architectural environment presents spatially distributed multi-sensory information: visual objects at specific locations, sound sources at specific locations, haptic surfaces at specific contact points, odour sources at specific positions. The brain must determine the spatial coherence of this multi-sensory array.
mechanism_chain.substrate: Modality-specific spatial processing: visual spatial maps (dorsal stream), auditory spatial maps (superior temporal cortex), haptic spatial maps (SI/SII), olfactory localization (nostrils, head movement)

data: Multi-sensory spatial information is processed by modality-specific neural systems
Visual spatial maps encode object locations (dorsal stream, parietal cortex)
Auditory spatial maps encode sound source locations (superior temporal cortex, IC)
Haptic spatial maps localize contact points (SI/SII cortex)
Olfactory localization is achieved through nostril comparison and head movement
justification.backing: Foundational neuroanatomy of spatial processing from Stein & Meredith (1993). Visual dorsal stream is established from Ungerleider & Mishkin (1982). Auditory spatial processing from King & Carlile (1993). Haptic spatial maps from Penfield & Boldrey (1937); modern confirmation via fMRI.
justification.qualifier: Confidence 0.6 reflects robust neural evidence across primate and human studies. MECHANISM warrant: direct neural pathways are anatomically documented.
justification.rebuttal: Under conditions of severe sensory degradation (aphantasia, deafness, severe neuropathy), some spatial channels may be non-functional, but alternative channels can partially compensate (see inverse effectiveness).
competing_accounts: Amodal perception hypothesis: spatial information is processed in a single amodal representation (weak evidence; channel-specific anatomy is clear)
Sensorimotor contingency account: space is constructed through action, not perception (compatible; motor output uses modality-specific maps)

mechanism_chain.process: Spatial rule of multisensory integration (Stein & Meredith, 1993): signals from the SAME spatial location are integrated (bound into a unified percept); signals from DIFFERENT spatial locations are segregated (processed as separate events). Spatial alignment is the primary binding cue for multi-sensory integration.
mechanism_chain.substrate: Superior colliculus spatial alignment; cortical multisensory areas

data: Superior colliculus multisensory neurons fire to stimuli from the SAME spatial location (integration)
Multisensory neurons show enhanced responses (>50% amplification) when stimuli are spatially aligned
Neurons show suppression or no response when stimuli are from different spatial locations
Spatial alignment window: ~30 cm (Stein & Meredith, 1993); ~200 ms temporal (Meredith et al., 1987)
This principle is conserved across species (cat, ferret, primate)
justification.backing: Stein & Meredith (1993) 'The Merging of the Senses' is foundational text with unit recording data from cat superior colliculus (multisensory neurons). Temporal window from Meredith et al. (1987) single-unit recording. Human behavioral analogues support spatial principle (Spence & Driver, 1997).
justification.qualifier: Confidence 0.6 reflects direct neural recording evidence in animals and consistent behavioral data in humans. MECHANISM warrant: neural mechanism for spatial binding is directly measured.
justification.rebuttal: The spatial window is not absolute; context and attention can modulate boundaries (Spence, 2011). Individual variability exists across observers.
competing_accounts: Temporal binding as primary principle: timing, not space, determines integration (partial; timing is also important but spatial alignment is primary in colliculus)
Feature binding through binding probability: probability is strictly Bayesian (compatible; Bayesian formalization builds on spatial-temporal constraints)
justification.panel_debate_reference: MULTI-I Panel, Feb 2026; Stein & Meredith authority (foundational)

mechanism_chain.process: Spatially coherent environments — where visual sources, sound sources, haptic surfaces, and olfactory signatures are spatially aligned — produce a unified percept of place. Spatial incoherence (sound from a different direction than the visual source, haptic properties that don't match the visible surface) produces perceptual fragmentation.
mechanism_chain.substrate: Multi-sensory integration → unified spatial representation vs. perceptual segregation

data: Spatially congruent environments (visual, auditory, haptic sources co-located) produce unified spatial percept
Spatially incongruent environments (sound from wrong direction, haptic properties don't match visual surface) produce perceptual fragmentation
Fragmentation is measurable: reduced spatial presence ratings, lower cognitive mapping accuracy, increased wayfinding errors
justification.backing: Spence (2011) review of crossmodal correspondences. Körding et al. (2007) Bayesian causal inference framework shows how incongruent spatial signals impair position estimation. Spatial presence literature (Witmer & Singer, 1998) shows coherence effects on presence.
justification.qualifier: Confidence 0.5 reflects behavioral and psychophysical evidence but not direct neural recording in humans under architectural conditions. EMPIRICAL_COVARIANCE warrant: correlations are measured but mechanisms partially inferred.
justification.rebuttal: Perceptual fragmentation may be task-dependent: some observers may ignore incongruent cues and focus on dominant channel. Individual differences in spatial weighting could moderate the effect.
competing_accounts: Selective attention: incongruence is ignored if bottom-up salience is low (partially true; automatic spatial binding still occurs)
Channel dominance account: vision always wins regardless of incongruence (refuted by numerous crossmodal studies)
justification.panel_debate_reference: MULTI-I Panel, Feb 2026; Spence authority; Körding et al. Bayesian framework

mechanism_chain.process: Perceptual fragmentation from spatial incoherence produces negative affect, reduced spatial presence, and impaired spatial memory encoding. Coherent environments produce positive affect, strong spatial presence, and enhanced spatial memory.
mechanism_chain.substrate: Coherence → affect pathway; interacts with MEMORY-I context encoding

data: Fragmentation from spatial incoherence produces negative affect: anxiety, unease, disorientation
Coherent environments produce positive affect: comfort, spatial legibility, place familiarity
Effect size: coherence produces d ≈ 0.25-0.40 improvement in spatial presence and affect ratings
Spatial presence supports spatial memory encoding: coherent spaces are recalled with higher accuracy
justification.backing: Spence (2011) on congruence and affect. Spatial presence literature (Witmer & Singer, 1998; Slater & Wilbur, 1997) on affect and presence. Memory-space interaction from Maguire et al. (1997) hippocampal place cells.
justification.qualifier: Confidence 0.45 reflects field studies and user ratings but mechanisms are partially inferred. CAPACITY warrant: functional capacity is measured (affect, memory) but neural mechanisms are theoretical.
justification.rebuttal: Affect effects may be mediated by expectation violations rather than coherence per se. Individual differences in spatial anxiety could moderate affect magnitude. Very familiar spaces may reduce coherence sensitivity.
competing_accounts: Cognitive load hypothesis: incongruence increases processing load, not specifically affects spatial coherence (compatible; a mechanism, not competing)
Novelty account: incongruence is negative only because it violates expectations (partially true but doesn't explain why coherent designs are inherently preferred)

spatial_alignment_window.interpretation: Multisensory signals within ~30 cm spatial and ~200 ms temporal window are bound (common cause inference). Outside this window, they are segregated.

coherence_affect_benefit.interpretation: Spatially coherent environments are rated ~0.25–0.40 standard deviations higher on spatial presence and place identity than incoherent environments.

value: displaced_audio (speakers not co-located with visual source)
artificial_scent_from_diffuser (olfactory signal not from visible material)
architectural_incoherence_sources.interpretation: Common architectural sources of spatial multi-sensory incoherence. Each source degrades the unified percept of place.

visual_impairment.effect: Spatial coherence becomes more dependent on auditory-haptic alignment. Displaced audio is more disorienting for visually impaired occupants who rely on sound for spatial localization.

IC2_AX4_interaction.IC2_body_budget: Spatial incoherence increases processing load (the brain must resolve conflicting spatial cues), which is a body budget cost. In allostatic deficit, the tolerance for spatial incoherence is reduced.
IC2_AX4_interaction.AX4_perceived_control: Spatial coherence is a prerequisite for environmental legibility. When multi-sensory spatial cues agree, the occupant can form a reliable spatial model and act on it (high control). When cues conflict, the spatial model is unreliable and action planning is impaired (low control).

name: Multi-Sensory Spatial Coherence in Architectural Environments

spatial_coherence_score.interpretation: Fraction of multi-sensory signals in the environment that are spatially co-located with their expected sources. Score of 1.0 = all sounds come from where they appear to originate, all material surfaces look and feel as expected.

audio_displacement_penalty.interpretation: Sound sources displaced from their visual origin (ceiling speakers for background music, hidden HVAC noise) degrade spatial coherence.

cross_template_interactions.description: Crossmodal congruence instantiates multisensory congruency principle
Crossmodal congruence enhances natural material perception
